This vignette compares the four frequentist regression models in `bayclumpr`. It also shows how to plot a calibration and reconstruct temperatures. If you're new to the package, start with `vignette("bayclumpr", package = "bayclumpr")`.

```{r setup}
library(bayclumpr)
```

## The four models

The models differ in which measurement errors they account for.

| Function | Model | Errors in `Temperature` | Errors in `D47` |
|:---------|:------|:-----------------------:|:---------------:|
| `cal.ols()` | Ordinary least squares | No | No |
| `cal.wols()` | Weighted least squares | No | No |
| `cal.deming()` | Deming regression (`deming` package) | Yes | Yes |
| `cal.york()` | York regression (`IsoplotR` package) | Yes | Yes |

The weights in `cal.wols()` don't come from the reported errors. They come from a regression of the absolute residuals on the fitted values, so observations in regions with more scatter get less weight. `cal.deming()` and `cal.york()` use `TempError` and `D47error` for each observation.

All four functions use bootstrapping. Each replicate resamples the calibration dataset with replacement and fits the model again. The result has one row per replicate, with the intercept (`alpha`) and slope (`beta`). We recommend at least 1,000 replicates.

## Fitting the models

We simulate 50 observations under the intermediate error scenario. The true values are `alpha` = 0.268 and `beta` = 0.0369.

```{r}
set.seed(3)
ds <- cal.dataset(error = "S2", nobs = 50)

fits <- list(
  OLS = cal.ols(data = ds, replicates = 1000),
  WOLS = cal.wols(data = ds, replicates = 1000),
  Deming = cal.deming(data = ds, replicates = 1000),
  York = cal.york(data = ds, replicates = 1000)
)
```

We summarize each model with the mean and 95% interval of the slope:

```{r}
t(sapply(fits, function(f) {
  c(alpha = mean(f$alpha),
    beta = mean(f$beta),
    beta_lower = quantile(f$beta, 0.025, names = FALSE),
    beta_upper = quantile(f$beta, 0.975, names = FALSE))
}))
```

## Plotting a calibration

`cal.ci()` takes the table of `alpha` and `beta` and returns the median line and its 95% interval over a range of temperatures. Here we plot the York calibration:

```{r}
ci <- cal.ci(fits$York, from = min(ds$Temperature), to = max(ds$Temperature))[[1]]

plot(D47 ~ Temperature, data = ds, pch = 16, col = "grey50",
     xlab = expression(10^6 / T^2 ~ (K)), ylab = expression(Delta[47]))
polygon(c(ci$x, rev(ci$x)), c(ci$ci_lower_est, rev(ci$ci_upper_est)),
        col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.3), border = NA)
lines(ci$x, ci$median_est, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
```

## Reconstructing temperatures

`rec.clumped()` reconstructs temperatures from any of these tables. We create a reconstruction dataset with three D47 values, each measured with two levels of precision:

```{r}
recData <- data.frame(
  Sample = paste("Sample", 1:6),
  D47 = rep(c(0.6, 0.7, 0.8), 2),
  D47error = rep(c(0.005, 0.02), each = 3)
)

rec.clumped(recData = recData, obCal = fits$York)
```

`meanTemp` is the temperature (°C) predicted from the mean slope and intercept. `error` is 1 SD. It combines the error in `D47` with the spread of slopes and intercepts in the bootstrap. It doesn't include the scatter of individual samples around the calibration line. The Bayesian reconstructions in `vignette("bayesian", package = "bayclumpr")` do include it.

We can also reconstruct the same samples under every model:

```{r}
recs <- lapply(fits, function(f) rec.clumped(recData = recData, obCal = f)$meanTemp)
cbind(recData, do.call(cbind, recs))
```
